Polyform tiling — validation ledger

Replicating Joseph Myers's plane-tiling classifications, then extending to seven new polyform families · updated 31 July 2026, 21:40
omino
kite
cairo

This project reimplements the tiling-classification algorithms described on Joseph Myers's polyform tiling page: for every polyform of a given size, decide whether it tiles the plane, and how simply — by translations alone, by 180° rotation (Conway criterion), isohedrally, or only k-anisohedrally — or prove it cannot tile at all. Everything below is computed by a single lattice-generic engine that now runs on all eleven Laves tilings: polyominoes, polykites, polyhexes and polyiamonds are validated cell-for-cell against Myers's published tables, and the same code then classifies seven families with no published classification — polycairos, polyrhombilles, polyflorets, polyprisms, polyaboloes, polydrafters and polypons.

Redelmeier enumeration of fixed shapes with canonical-aspect deduplication to free shapes; hole detection by complement flood-fill. Agrees with Myers (and OEIS A000105) at every point tested.

Stage 2 · completeTranslation & 180° tilings validated

A lattice tiling exists iff the tile is a transversal of the cells modulo some index-n/c sublattice (Hermite-normal-form enumeration); a p2 tiling likewise on the index-2n/c quotient with a 180° rotation adjoined. Matches all four of Myers's columns, including the subtle translation-only shapes (first at n = 9).

Stage 3 · completeFull classification: isohedral, anisohedral, non-tilers n ≤ 10 validated

Candidate wallpaper subgroups of the base tiling's symmetry group are enumerated as (point subgroup, invariant sublattice, offset cocycle) triples modulo conjugacy; a k-isohedral tiling is a k-orbit exact cover of the quotient torus. Non-tiling is proved separately by possible-neighbour arc-consistency pruning, corona elimination, and a depth-d surround search (Myers's method). Every free polyomino through n = 10 is now classified, and every number below matches Myers's tables — all 4,655 10-ominoes in 204 s on 8 cores.

The k-breakdown column reads "k:count" — e.g. at n = 9 there are eight 2-anisohedral nonominoes and one 4-anisohedral (Myers: 8 + 1). The engine also computes certified Heesch lower bounds by depth-d surround search on unpruned neighbour lists (the pruned lists used for non-tiling proofs are unsound for Heesch, as Myers notes): of the three non-tiling heptominoes, two have Heesch ≥ 1 and one — the plus-with-tail — cannot even be surrounded once (Heesch 0), matching the known values.

Stage 4 · completePolykites n ≤ 10 validated

The [3.4.6.4] Laves (kite) backend passes its machine-checked group axioms; free counts match Myers exactly (1, 2, 4, 10, 27, 85, 262, 873). Classification agrees with Myers's kite tables at every entry through n = 8, including the famously sparse structure — no translation or 180°-only tilings except at multiples of the residue count, the lone 3-anisohedral 5-kite, and exactly one shape the classifier cannot resolve at n = 8 (see below). Kites found this engine's first bug: neighbour placements must be genuine symmetries of the Laves tiling, which is invisible on the square grid where every integer translation is one.

The n = 10 row (added 31 July) is a triple event. First, agreement with Myers holds at every column — 702 holey shapes, 9,294 non-tilers, and not one 10-kite that tiles by translation, 180° or isohedrally. Second, of Myers's fifteen anisohedral entries our classifier leaves three unresolved at kmax 4, and exact k = 5 searches plus k = 6 covers settle two of them as the family's first 6-anisohedral polykites — kites join the rhombilles, florets and polypons in the isohedral-number-6 club — which the 13-rhombille probes then grew to twenty-three shapes across four Laves families. Third, the last unresolved 10-kite is the turtle — the hat's aperiodic sibling from the same 2023 paper: no k-isohedral tiling for any k ≤ 8, yet the SAT surround engine finds coronas to depth 7 in seconds (certified Heesch lower bound ≥ 7). Myers's tables contain exactly two aperiodic polykites; the engine has now rediscovered both, each as the unique unresolved shape of its size.

The three 10-kites that resisted standard classification. Left and middle: the first 6-anisohedral polykites (k ≤ 5 exhausted, 6-orbit tilings found). Right: the turtle, rediscovered the same way the hat was — no k-isohedral tiling for any k ≤ 8, coronas to depth 7 and counting.

Stage 5 · completeThe hat, rediscovered aperiodicity evidence

Classifying all 873 free 8-kites left exactly one shape unresolved — and it is the hat, the aperiodic monotile of Smith, Myers, Kaplan and Goodman-Strauss (2023). The engine wasn't told about it; it simply survived every classification the engine knows, which is precisely the computational signature of aperiodicity Myers describes:

  • It tiles locally: surrounds (coronas) exist to depth 6 and counting — a certified Heesch lower bound of 6, with no failure in sight (the true value is ∞, since it tiles the plane).
  • But never periodically: exhaustive search over all candidate wallpaper subgroups finds no tiling with isohedral number k for any k ≤ 7 (each exact-k search closes in seconds; positive controls: the engine finds the 4-anisohedral nonomino and 3-anisohedral kites).

A shape that surrounds indefinitely but admits no k-isohedral tiling at any searched k is either aperiodic or extraordinarily anisohedral — Myers's programs would "run for ever" on it; ours reports it unresolved and hands over exactly this evidence. The same signature has since singled out the turtle among the 10-kites (Stage 4) — the engine has now rediscovered both of the known aperiodic polykites blind.

Stage 6 · new resultsPolycairos terra incognita, classified

The Cairo backend models the tiling as the dual of the snub square tiling on an exact integer lattice (four pentagon aspects, p4g symmetry with its glide offsets handled by the group cocycles). Free polycairo counts match OEIS A159866 (1, 2, 5, 17, 55, 206, 781, 3099, …) — and beyond enumeration, the tiling classification below appears to be new data: we found no published tiling classification of polycairos.

This family is the project's goldmine. Every rhombus is two triangles of a finer triangular lattice, so each polyrhombille is also a polyiamond — and every hard case below does tile the plane as a free polyiamond, just never in a rhombille-aligned way (the standard convention here, cf. Myers's identical caveat for the 1-kite). Deep probes resolved all three resistant pentarhombilles as 6-anisohedral: no aligned tiling has fewer than six orbits, yet each tiles with six orbits under a pure translation lattice (verified below). For scale, polyominoes first reach isohedral number 6 at n = 14 — these do it with five rhombi. One of the three uses only rotational aspects, so its chirally-notched version is an honest unmarked tile with isohedral number 6; the other two need reflected copies (both are proven Spectre-mode non-tilers). The 7-rhombille and seven 11-rhombilles follow the same pattern — and n = 13's probes (31 July) added five more, giving sixteen isohedral-number-6 shapes in this one family. At n = 10 and 11 the anisohedral spectrum is strictly bimodal: every anisohedral shape has k = 3 or 6, never 2, 4, or 5 (indeed no 10-rhombille tiles isohedrally at all); k = 2 reappears at the even size 12, yet at n = 13 the six ceiling holds — five of the thirteen anisohedral shapes reach it, and the four resistant shapes that don't tile were each dispatched by SAT surround exhaustion at depth 3.

Resolved (30 July, afternoon): the star does not tile. As a free 20-iamond it tiles by mere translation, but aligned to the rhombille grid it is a proven non-tiler with Heesch number exactly 3 — and, as a posthumous consistency check, a SAT version of the k-orbit search has since pushed its periodic exclusion from k ≤ 15 (4.3 CPU-hours of backtracking) to k ≤ 18 in seven minutes, with every group refutation through k = 15 DRAT-certified. The proof came from a new attack: encode depth-d surround existence as SAT (placements as variables; per-cell at-most-one; corona coverage forced level by level) and hand it to a CDCL solver. Where the recursive search had burned 95M nodes across seven cores without finishing even one of thirty top-level branches, cadical settles depth 3 in 0.2 seconds: a surround exists (88 tiles — the patch below, independently verified and re-certified by the original search engine as a warm start). Depth 4 is UNSAT in 7 seconds (confirmed by a second solver, and identical over the raw un-pruned candidate universe): no depth-4 surround exists, so the star cannot tile, and its aligned Heesch number is exactly 3 — between the two coronas everyone could find and the four nobody could. The SAT method agrees with the recursive engine on every validation case, in both directions, with ~500× speedups on exhaustive verdicts. And the negative direction is now machine-certified: the depth-4 refutation (in both the pruned and raw candidate universes) carries a DRAT proof log verified by the independent checker drat-trim, so the verdict rests only on the encoding (itself cross-validated against the recursive engine) and a 3,000-line C checker — not on solver trust. At that moment every shape then computed, in every family, stood resolved except the hat — whose “unresolved” verdict is itself the right answer, being the computational signature of the aperiodic monotile. The frontier has since moved: new rows at kite n = 10 (where the same signature found the turtle), hex n = 8 and rhombille n = 13 opened fresh unresolved shapes, and the SAT probes working through them have so far only added tilers and non-tilers, no new mysteries — and the nine 13-rhombilles have since resolved too: five 6-anisohedral, four proven non-tilers, nothing open in the family.

The star 10-rhombille: tiles the plane by translation as a free 20-iamond, but rhombille-aligned it is a proven non-tiler with Heesch number exactly 3.
The star’s maximal surround, found by the SAT engine in 0.2 s: the center (dark) wrapped in three complete coronas (blues), with outer filler tiles (gold/orange) supporting the third. No fourth corona exists (UNSAT, 7 s) — Heesch number 3, hence a non-tiler.
The unresolved pentarhombilles as first found (left, middle still open; right since resolved as the 6-anisohedral shape). Each tiles the plane only by breaking alignment with the underlying rhombille grid.
The minimal (6-orbit) aligned tiling of the 6-anisohedral pentarhombille, colored by orbit — its symmetry group is translations only, and no aligned tiling of this five-rhombus shape has fewer than six orbits. Verified overlap-free from the exact-cover solution.

Stage 8 · new resultsPolyflorets — a chiral family classified n ≤ 11

The floret pentagonal ([3.3.3.3.6] Laves) tiling is chiral — its symmetry group p6 contains no reflections — so polyflorets are one-sided: mirror images are genuinely different shapes. The backend models the dual snub trihexagonal tiling exactly, via the index-7 Loeschian sublattice ⟨(2,1),(−1,3)⟩ of the triangular lattice. Three free dominoes, as predicted by the snub tiling's three p6 edge orbits. Also new: polyhex and polyiamond backends validate the engine against two more of Myers's table sets — now complete: hexes n ≤ 6 and iamonds n ≤ 7 exact. The last hexahex holdout was proven a non-tiler by a two-hour exhaustive depth-5 surround search. The heptahexes tell the same story at n = 7: all columns match Myers. Three deep non-tilers were proven at depth 5; the last two had hit their node budgets inconclusively and were parked — until the SAT surround engine (built for the star, below) settled all five unresolved heptahexes as proven non-tilers in seconds (surrounds exhaust at depths 2–4, each with a DRAT-certified refutation), matching Myers exactly. Polyhex n = 7 is now fully resolved. The octahexes (n = 8, 1,448 shapes) extend the validation and are now fully resolved: every column matches Myers exactly — 209 translation, 721 by 180°, 88 isohedral, all 36 anisohedral shapes (27 2-, 7 3-, 2 4-anisohedral), and all 381 non-tilers, the last nine of which fell to SAT surround exhaustion in seconds apiece (depths 2–3, results/probe_octahex_sat.log). A follow-up SAT sweep then pinned each one's exact Heesch number over the engine's raw candidate universe: 2, 2, 3, 2, 2 (in hex-7.json's unresolved order) — four of the five max out at two coronas, one at three (results/sat_heptahex_heesch.log).

The floret grid is spectacularly tiling-hostile: not a single 5-floret tiles the plane (79 non-tilers, 1 hole), and through n = 8 there were no anisohedral polyflorets at all. The streak finally breaks at n = 9: the five smallest anisohedral polyflorets (all 2-anisohedral) emerge among 14,561 shapes.

n = 10 is a near-total cliff. Of 55,624 free 10-florets (7,948 with holes), exactly two tile the plane — every other shape is a proven non-tiler. And neither survivor is simple: one is the family's first 3-anisohedral floret, and the other is 6-anisohedral — the kmax-4 classification left it unresolved, an exact k = 5 search then excluded five orbits, and a 6-orbit tiling was found and verified overlap-free (below). That ties the pentarhombille record for the highest isohedral number in the project (matched again by four polypons in Stage 12) — this time on the chiral p6 grid, where aligned tilings can never use reflections at all.

And n = 11 completes the collapse: of 213,951 free 11-florets, not one tiles the plane — 37,159 have holes and the remaining 176,792 are all proven non-tilers, with nothing unresolved. The same n = 11 dead zone strikes the drafters and the polypons (Stages 11–12).

The only two 10-florets that tile: the first 3-anisohedral polyfloret (left) and the 6-anisohedral 10-floret (right, tinted).
The minimal (6-orbit) tiling of the 6-anisohedral 10-floret, colored by orbit — the tiling's symmetry group is translations only, and no aligned tiling of this shape has fewer than six orbits (k ≤ 5 exhausted). Verified overlap-free from the exact-cover solution.

Stage 10 · new resultsPolyaboloes (kisquadrille tans) classified n ≤ 11

Classical polyaboloes are built from tans — half-square right triangles — and a tan is exactly a pair of tetrakis-square ("kisquadrille") quarter-triangles glued along a half-diagonal. So polyaboloes enumerate as tan-pair regions on the [4.8.8] Laves substrate (deduped by union: the two matchings of a full square are one shape), and the counts match OEIS A006074 (1, 3, 4, 14, 30, 107, 318). Classification is with respect to kisquadrille-aligned tilings, as elsewhere on this page.

Every abolo through n = 4 tiles the plane; the first anisohedral polyaboloes arrive at n = 7 (eight 2-anisohedral, two 3-anisohedral). The enneabolo question is settled for this grid: exhaustive sweeps of all 3,743 enneaboloes (kmax 6) and all 7,448 one-sided enneaboloes in Spectre mode (kmax 7) find a maximum anisohedral number of 4 with reflections (a single 4-anisohedral enneabolo) and only 2 without — no ≥6-anisohedral enneabolo exists under kisquadrille-aligned tilings in either convention. If the reported example is real, it likely lives on the kisrhombille ([4.6.12]) grid — classified in Stage 11. The n = 11 row (46,476 shapes, fully resolved) brings the family's largest anisohedral crop yet: 105 shapes, five of them 3-anisohedral.

Stage 11 · new resultsPolydrafters (kisrhombille) free n ≤ 12, one-sided n ≤ 9

The kisrhombille ([4.6.12] Laves) tiling of 30-60-90 triangles — drafter country. This family is edge-to-edge polydrafters (cells joined along full shared grid edges; the classical polydrafter census also counts other contacts). Like florets, the grid is hostile: no 5- or (below) odd-one-sided drafter tiles. Maximum anisohedral number found through n = 12: 3 (seven 3-anisohedral 10-drafters) — so no ≥6-anisohedral shape here either, in either mode. Strikingly, not one 11-drafter tiles; tiling resumes at n = 12, where all eight anisohedral shapes are 2-anisohedral.

Chirality parity: in Spectre mode not even the single drafter tiles — the kisrhombille tiling needs both mirror forms of its own cell. The pattern in the table has a clean proof: rotations preserve a drafter's handedness, the grid is half left-handed and half right-handed, so a one-sided shape with unequal L/R cell counts can never tile without reflections — and every odd-size shape is unbalanced. The engine's per-shape proofs confirm the theorem case by case.

Stage 12 · new resultsPolypons (triakis triangular) — the last Laves tiling free n ≤ 14, one-sided n ≤ 12

The triakis triangular ([3.12.12] Laves) tiling splits each triangle of the regular triangular tiling into three 30-30-120 obtuse triangles; its polyforms are the classical polypons, and this backend completes the set — all eleven Laves tilings now run on the one engine. Enumeration is validated externally at every point computed: free counts match OEIS A057784 (1, 2, 2, 4, 4, 10, 13, 29, 47, 100, 181, 383, 738, 1539) and one-sided counts match A151531 exactly. But we found no published tiling classification of polypons in either mode, so the tables below appear to be new data.

The family runs the project's whole dramatic arc in miniature. A total wipeout at n = 5 — all four pentapons are non-tilers, and so are all seven one-sided ones — then the first translation tilers at n = 6, and a long stretch where nothing anisohedral exists. At n = 10 the ceiling breaks: the first anisohedral polypons (one 2- and one 3-anisohedral) — and all three decapons that resisted standard classification are proven 6-anisohedral (for each, k ≤ 5 is exhausted and a 6-orbit tiling found), an exact echo of the three resistant pentarhombilles. One of the three tiles with six orbits in both the full and the one-sided convention — its minimal tiling is a pure translation lattice (below) — so it carries the pentarhombille's corollary: its chirally-notched version is an honest unmarked tile with isohedral number 6. The other two need reflected copies; their one-sided versions are proven non-tilers. At n = 11 exactly one of 181 shapes tiles at all, and it is 3-anisohedral; the one-sided 11-pons are wiped out entirely (356 of 356 are non-tilers). Then n = 12 normalizes (34 translation, 11 180°-only, 91 isohedral) and n = 13 is isohedral-or-nothing, before n = 14 brings nine anisohedral shapes: four 2-, four 3-anisohedral, and a resistant since proven the family's fourth 6-anisohedral tile (k ≤ 5 exhausted, 6-orbit tiling verified). With the sixteen rhombilles, the 10-floret and the two 10-kites, the project now has twenty-three shapes of isohedral number 6, across four Laves families — and every free polypon through n = 14, and every one-sided one through n = 12, is resolved.

Stage 13 · new resultsSpectre mode: reflections banned seven families

Chiral edge notches (as on the Spectre) enforce grid alignment and orientation, so classification under direct isometries only — rotations and translations, shapes one-sided — is the version realizable by an honest unmarked notched tile, with no grid caveat. The engine's direct mode is validated against the one-sided polyomino counts (A000988: 1, 1, 2, 7, 18, 60, 196, 704 exact). A uniform new result: all eleven 4-anisohedral polycairos (n = 7, 9, 11) are Spectre-mode non-tilers in both chiralities — every minimal 4-orbit tiling in the Cairo family depends on reflections. Highlights: the 6-anisohedral pentarhombille survives unchanged (its minimal tiling is translations-only), so its notched version is an unmarked tile with isohedral number 6; the two long-unresolved pentarhombilles are Spectre-mode non-tilers in both chiralities (exact direct-Heesch numbers 1 and 2) — any aligned tiling they admit must mix mirror-image copies; and all five isohedral heptaboloes lose their tilings when reflections are banned (their one-sided versions are non-tilers or 2-anisohedral). The seventh family, the polypons, is classified one-sided in Stage 12 — where exactly one of the three 6-anisohedral decapons keeps a reflection-free six-orbit tiling, and the other two become non-tilers.

The one-sided hat is a proven non-tiler. Running the polykites in Spectre mode (below) resolves every one-sided shape through n = 8 — including the hat, whose one-sided version is killed by the surround search. This independently establishes the known fact that every aligned hat tiling must contain reflected hats (which is why the Spectre required the equilateral Tile(1,1), not a polykite). The 3-anisohedral 5-kite likewise needs reflections: all 48 one-sided 5-kites are non-tilers.

One-sided polyprisms have a structural story: the prismatic grid's only direct point symmetry is the half-turn, so every reflection-free tiling is of translation or p2 type — and empirically through n = 8 there are no anisohedral one-sided polyprisms at all.

Stage 14 · new resultsWang decorations: bump/dent matching rules third audit closed · v3 oracle-verified

The engine supports edge decorations: every boundary edge of a shape carries a label — 0 is neutral (matches itself), labels 1 and 2 are bump/dent partners that match only each other, exactly the Wang-tile mechanism behind the Spectre’s notches. The question this machinery answers: what do decorations do to a shape’s isohedral number? It took three audits to earn a trustworthy answer.

How this section was wrong twice. The first release showed a decorated L-tromino “4-anisohedral” tiling with overlapping bump discs; a reader flagged it, and the overlaps turned out to be bump-meets-bump contacts in a phantom tiling — the validator’s translate window missed touching pairs under skewed sublattice bases (too permissive). The v2 rerun fixed that and was promptly caught the other way: a reader observed that the new “4-orbit” figure looked transitive, and brute force agreed — orbit count 1. Placements had been identified by cell footprint, which conflates the mirror aspects of a symmetric shape; the decoder could pick the label-wrong aspect and reject genuine covers, silently inflating every k (too strict). The v3 engine keys placements by label class, decodes orbits from seeds by the group action, keeps the independent patch-level post-check on every success — and every positive below has been re-verified by a brute-force orbit-count oracle that computes the found tiling’s full decorated symmetry group from scratch: 160 of 160 k = 2 verdicts exact, zero violations.

The parity lemma (unchanged, and doing most of the work): with the identity mirror action, a decoration whose bump-count differs from its dent-count for any bump/dent pair tiles at no k whatsoever — bumps and dents must pair up across shared edges, and every tile carries the same labels. On an eight-edge shape this dismisses 5,454 of 6,561 three-label decorations before any search runs.

The v3 truth is more rigid than either wrong version. All eleven Laves unit prototiles — the hexagon included, contrary to v2’s prized “k = 3 hexagon” — are decoration-rigid: every 3-label bump/dent decoration either leaves the prototile isohedral or kills every tiling within the search bound; nothing in between. (The rhombus keeps its clean geometric rule: it tiles iff each edge pair meeting at a wide corner is self-compatible.) The polyominoes manage exactly one notch of the ladder: the domino is rigid too ({1}), while the L-tromino, I-tromino and O-tetromino each have a genuine population of 2-anisohedral decorations (80, 48 and 32 of 6,561) — a bump/dent rule can double the isohedral number of a translation-friendly shape, and, as far as every sound sweep so far can see, no 3-label decoration of any shape tested exceeds k = 2. Richer alphabets don’t help: 5-label sweeps (two independent bump/dent pairs) of the hexagon and domino produce more isohedral decorations and nothing anisohedral at all. The open question flipped: earlier drafts asked whether the hexagon’s “ceiling of 3” was real; the real question is whether any edge-matching decoration of any polyform can beat 2 — and if one can, how large it has to be.

Genuine at last: a minimal 2-orbit decorated L-tromino tiling — labels (0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2), a single bump and dent on two of eight edges (sorted-edge order), one of the eighty 2-anisohedral decorations in decor-L-tromino-v3. One disc per matched edge, in the bump-carrier’s orbit colour; the undecorated shape tiles by translation, and the oracle confirms no tiling compatible with this decoration has fewer than two orbits.

A methodological coda: v1’s bug could only accept too much, v2’s could only reject too much, and each produced a plausible-looking mathematical narrative — spectra with “gaps”, a special hexagon — that dissolved under an independent check the search code had no hand in. The surviving facts are duller and firmer: rigidity everywhere, one honest doubling, and a pre-filter lemma that does more than the search does.

Stage 15Roadmap

  • resolvedDecoration engine, third audit (v3) Fixed (label-class placement identity, seed-based orbit decoding) and fully re-swept; every positive re-verified by the brute-force orbit-count oracle (160/160 exact). Verdict: all k ≥ 3 decoration claims were phantoms — the true ceiling everywhere tested is k = 2, and all eleven unit prototiles are decoration-rigid.
  • resolvedThe new frontier: kite 10 / hex 8 / rhombille 13 All twenty-one probes closed: kite n = 10 gave two 6-anisohedral kites and the turtle; all nine octahexes are proven non-tilers (hex n = 8 fully matches Myers); the nine 13-rhombilles split five 6-anisohedral / four non-tilers. Isohedral-number-6 club: twenty-three shapes.
  • resolvedSAT for the k-orbit search itself Delivered: per-group UNSAT queries with cardinality bounds; validated on five known min-k cases; the star’s exclusion extended to k ≤ 18 in ~7 minutes (the old engine took 4.3 CPU-hours for k ≤ 15, which is now DRAT-certified). Exclusion sweeps should move to SAT; the backtracking engine stays for cheap positives.
  • resolvedFourth subtlety: “bogus orbits” audit The SAT work uncovered that wrap-around placements whose torus footprint is fixed setwise can enter covers that double-cover the plane — a false-positive risk only. The audit is done: all 37 stored anisohedral examples across every family were re-derived by the SAT engine with bogus orbits forbidden and plane-level cross-checks; every minimum matched its published k exactly (results/audit_positive_examples.log).
  • resolvedThe star 10-rhombille Settled: proven non-tiler, aligned Heesch number exactly 3 — depth-3 surround found and depth-4 refuted by the SAT surround engine (see the rhombille stage). The project’s flagship question, closed.
  • resolvedThe deep heptahexes All five unresolved heptahexes proven non-tilers by SAT surround exhaustion (depths 2–4), matching Myers. Polyhex n = 7 fully resolved.
  • supersededDecoration sweeps, v2 All sweeps were rerun under the window-fixed validator — but the third audit (above) then showed the search can also reject genuine covers, so v2’s spectra (domino {1, 3}, trominoes {1, 2, 4}, O-tetromino {1, 2, 3}, hexagon k = 3) stand only as upper-bound data pending v3.
  • resolvedDRAT-checked UNSAT proofs Done: the star’s depth-4 refutation (both universes) and all five heptahex exhaustions carry DRAT proofs verified by drat-trim, with negative controls. One gotcha for posterity: pysat’s cadical bindings accept with_proof=True but silently emit empty proofs — the pipeline hard-fails on that and uses glucose42.

How the engine works

One engine, eleven grids. Every base tiling is described combinatorially: cells are integer points, the tiling's symmetries act as affine integer maps, and a backend only supplies the codes, matrices and cell polygons (adjacency is derived and the group axioms are machine-checked — no floating point anywhere). A periodic tiling by a shape P with symmetry group G ⊆ W collapses to a finite statement: the images of P under G's finitely many coset representatives must exactly partition the torus of cells modulo G's translation sublattice. So tiling questions become exact-cover problems over enumerated subgroups — one orbit for isohedral, k orbits for k-isohedral — and non-tiling is proved separately by Myers's neighbour-pruning, corona elimination and depth-d surround search. This differs from Myers's own class-based backtracking implementation, which makes the replication a genuinely independent check of his tables.

The SAT pivot. Both hard search regimes turned out to be CDCL-solver territory. Surround existence: placements become Boolean variables; each grid cell gets an at-most-one constraint over the placements covering it; corona membership is forced level by level, so “a depth-d surround exists” is one satisfiability query over a placement universe provably closed under everything the recursive search could reach. The star's depth-3 question — hours of inconclusive backtracking — became a 0.2-second SAT call, and its depth-4 refutation a 7-second UNSAT. Periodic exclusion: per candidate group, orbit masks become variables, every torus cell gets an exactly-one constraint, and a cardinality bound at the group's admissible k makes one UNSAT query exclude every k at once; the star's k-exclusion moved from 4.3 CPU-hours (k ≤ 15) to seven minutes (k ≤ 18). Positive answers decode to concrete tilings and are re-verified independently; negative answers emit DRAT proof logs checked by drat-trim, so refutations no longer rest on trusting any search code — ours or the solver's.

The audit trail. This page's numbers have survived four soundness episodes, two of them caught by a reader of the figures, and it seems more honest to display that history than to bury it. (1) An instrumentation ambiguity let node-budget cap-hits be read as found surrounds — caught in an internal audit; every claim was re-derived and the reporting disambiguated. (2) The decorated-tiling validator checked label compatibility over a fixed window of lattice translates in Hermite coordinates; skewed bases let genuinely touching tiles escape the window, and phantom decorated tilings slipped through — caught by a reader noticing overlapping bump discs, which turned out to be bump-meets-bump contacts no valid tiling could contain. Fixed with a Gauss-reduced basis, a span-derived window, and an independent patch-level post-check on every decorated success. (3) Decorated placements were identified by their cell footprint, which conflates mirror aspects whose labels differ; the decoder could pick the wrong aspect and reject genuine covers, inflating decorated isohedral numbers — caught by a reader observing that a published “4-orbit” tiling looked transitive (it was; brute force confirms orbit count 1). The v3 engine keys placements by label class and verifies every positive against a brute-force orbit-count oracle. (4) The SAT cross-checks exposed that a wrap-around placement whose torus footprint is merely setwise-stabilized can enter an “orbit” whose plane expansion double-covers — a false-positive-only risk; the systematic re-audit came back clean (all 37 stored anisohedral examples re-derived exactly). The pattern worth stating: every bug was found because some independent artifact — a figure, a cross-check, a second engine — contradicted the search, which is the strongest argument this project knows for computing everything twice.

Engine: ~/src/polyform, branch engine · Python; SAT via PySAT (glucose42/cadical), UNSAT proofs checked by drat-trim · Reference: J. Myers, Polyform tiling, polyomino.org.uk (retrieved 29 July 2026).
